newsitem.title: UK: Firm dollar hits international vegetable oil trade.
newsitem.headline: Firm dollar hits international vegetable oil trade.

text.p: At this time of year European vegetable oil market traders would normally be focusing on Chicago soy futures where exaggerated price movements can often occur in reaction to changes in U.S.Midwest weather patterns.
However, this year dollar firmness has ruled the international vegetable oil market, limiting both up and downside price movements.
"Cash (vegoils) markets always react slower than futures to any changes but this year it has at times gone against the Chicago trend owing to the firm dollar," said one trader.

Soft oils are traded in Dutch guilders a 100 kilos on the benchmark Rotterdam market while soybeans are bought by crushers in dollars a tonne. This limits the downside of the oils market when the U.S. currency is firm and Chicago futures have turned bearish on good weather conditions.
When the Chicago market swings the other way crushers find themselves with a different problem as margins are squeezed by more expensive soybeans and the firm dollar.
But at the same time buyers refuse to pay more because they know that sooner or later sellers will have to crack owing to the over-supply of edible oils in the market at present.
"People always have it on their minds that speculators play with the soy futures at this time of year and at the end of the day the crop will probably come to no harm," said one trader.
In the palm oil market the firm dollar against the Malaysian ringgit could be good news as it makes' palm oil more attractive on the export market.
The Malaysian market is faced with rising output and low exports.

Stocks of palm oil look set to reach one million tonnes by September/October, but with the firm dollar making palm oil cheaper for importers, traders are hopping that major buyers, like India, Pakistan and maybe China may be tempted to jump in while prices are low in dollar terms.
However, there is little sign of this happening at the moment.

In his latest crop report Malaysian private forecaster Ivan Wong projected July palm oil output at 630,000 to 635,000 tonnes while figures from cargo surveyor SGS put exports for the first twenty five days for July at 580,610 tonnes.
It's similar story among lauric oils with markets faced with rising production seemingly being thrown a lifeline by a firm dollar which could make exports cheaper.
But falling coconut oil prices could lead to Indonesia reducing exports, triggering higher prices towards the end of the year.
"The market in general is behaving very oddly for this time of year, mainly due to the dollar, and at times it is very difficult to know where it is," said one trader.
